title: Every joint owes charity
hookLine: each day each joint owes charity: making peace, helping someone mount, a good word, each step to prayer, removing harm (Nawawi 26, Abu Hurayrah)
tomorrow: where do you look when nobody can tell you what's right?

cards: Your body owes something every morning. What, and to whom? Crack your knuckles, roll your shoulders, bend a knee.
Before coffee, before the phone, your body has bent and lifted and turned more times than you'd guess. No one sends that bill; it comes with being alive.
In al-Nawawi's twenty-sixth hadith, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says each of those joints owes a charity, every day the sun rises. Not money. Something smaller, and everywhere.

teach.b: From Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, told by Abu Hurayrah, in paraphrase: every joint of a person owes charity each day the sun rises. Making peace between two people is charity.
Helping someone onto their ride, or lifting their things up to them, is charity. A good word is charity. Every step you take to prayer is charity.
Moving something harmful off the road is charity. Five payments, and none costs a cent. Here's what it gives you for an ordinary week: a list.
Two coworkers arguing over a schedule? Make peace, and the debt's paid. A neighbor wrestling a suitcase into a trunk?
Lift. A friend's long, anxious text? A good word.
The walk to whatever prayer you keep. A broken bottle on the sidewalk? Move it.
None of it needs a title, a budget or a plan. Just eyes that notice.

teach.h: PEACE, A LIFT, A WORD, A STEP.
teach.b: Something to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, the walk to prayer counts step by step.

teach.h: MOVE THE HARM OFF THE ROAD.

teach.b: Every joint of every person: the hadith starts from the body all humans share, whatever they believe.
The Qur'an says it to everyone: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another."
One body, one daily bill, and small change to pay it with everywhere.

how: Muslims teach this hadith with its everyday list, and many count small acts, such as moving litter or a stone off a path or carrying someone's bags, as charity in this sense.

games.q: what does “every joint owes charity” mean?
o: a health rule about stretching each morning
the body's daily debt, paid in small kind acts
a tax on wealth that's paid once a year

games.q: five ways to pay — tap the pairs.

s: the joints' charity has to be paid in money
peace, a lift, a good word, a step to prayer, moving harm off the road.
moving something harmful off the road counts as charity
it's the last item on the hadith's list.
the hadith's debt is owed only on special days

games.q: on your break, you see a coworker struggling with a heavy box. what's this hadith's view?
o: lift it: helping someone with their load is charity.
it isn't your job, and your break belongs to you.
help only if a manager is around to notice it.
games.why: helping someone onto their ride, or lifting their things up to them, is on the hadith's list.

practice: Write one person a good word, a real one: something they did well, something you noticed, a thank-you that's overdue. Keep it short, send it, then set the phone face down and rest your hands for the rest of the sit.
A good word is one of the hadith's five payments.

wordCard.voice: Every joint owes charity: the sulama, the joints, each owing a small gift a day. Peace, a lift, a good word, a step, a cleared path.

orig.note: Arabic: the joints or small bones of the body; each owes a charity a day.

carryVoice: Your line: every joint, every day. Paid every morning, in small change that nobody else is counting. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 26; Sahih al-Bukhari 2989, Sahih Muslim 1009 (Abu Hurayrah)
